newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CS Private Banking sees Sfr interest rates stable.
newsitem.headline: CS Private Banking sees Sfr interest rates stable.

text.p: The head of investment analysis at Credit Suisse Private Banking said he thought Swiss interest rates would move sideways for the rest of the year before rising slightly in 1998.
Swiss interest rates seem near a low point in this business cycle, Alexander Galli told the Finanz und Wirtschaft newspaper in an interview published on Saturday.

"But the leeway for rates on the long end to go down does not seem completely exausted because the Swiss economy will hardly leave the stagnation phase in 1997 and inflation is less than one percent," he said.
Real long-term rates of 2 to 2.5 percent are still relatively high, while one percent seems close to the lower limit in the money market, he said.

"I thus expect a sideways movement of money and capital market rates in Switzerland that could lead to a slight increase next year. This is also true if the economy starts growing again in 1998 and inflation fears perhaps arise," he said.
"But I don't see a significant change in interest rates because marked increases are not expected in either the United States or Germany," he added.
Galli said the discount rate was already at an extraordinarily low level of 1.0 percent, but it was possible the Swiss National Bank would cut it again.

"A further reduction -- for example to 0.5 percent -- would not change anything about monetary policy given the massive expansion of money on offer already, but would show the National Bank's will to do its utmost to support the...Swiss economy.
"If it does this, it has at most symbolic value because demand for discount credits has never had much significance for monetary policy," he said.
